pharm: Parenteral magnesium salt acting as a physiologic calcium antagonist; CNS depressant and smooth-muscle relaxant that blocks neuromuscular transmission to prevent and treat eclamptic seizures.
quick: Eclampsia: IV load 4-6 g over 15-20 min, then 1-2 g/hr infusion
Used for eclampsia/pre-eclampsia; avoid prolonged use >5-7 days (fetal hypocalcemia/bone effects)
Compatible; excreted in milk in small amounts
Reduce dose; toxic accumulation risk (4 g load, 1 g/hr, max 20 g/48h)
Patellar reflex, respiratory rate, urine output, serum Mg, renal function
summary: Parenteral magnesium sulphate is the agent of choice for preventing and treating seizures in pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, and is also used for torsades de pointes and hypomagnesemia. It acts as a physiologic calcium antagonist and CNS depressant. The principal hazard is dose-related toxicity (loss of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory depression, cardiac arrest); the antidote is IV calcium (calcium gluconate). Requires bedside monitoring of patellar reflexes, respiratory rate, and urine output before each repeated dose.
indications: Treatment of seizures and prevention of recurrent seizures in eclampsia
Treatment of acute and chronic hypomagnesemia
Magnesium supplementation in total parenteral nutrition

dosage.d: Loading 4-6 g over 15-20 min, then 1-2 g/hr
dosage.n: Max 30-40 g/24h; do not continue beyond 5-7 days (fetal toxicity)

dosage.t: Into alternate buttocks every 4 h as needed
dosage.n: Often combined with an IV loading dose

dosage.t: May repeat; followed by infusion if needed
dosage.n: Not specified in FDA label; standard clinical reference dosing

dosage.d: 5 g (~40 mEq) in 1 L of D5W or 0.9% NaCl
dosage.n: Or up to 250 mg/kg IM within a 4 h period
Max 20 g/48h; monitor serum Mg closely

admin: Dilute IV solutions to a concentration of 20% or less before administration
Give the loading dose slowly (4-6 g over 15-20 minutes); rapid IV bolus can cause hypotension and asystole
Deep IM injection of undiluted 50% solution is acceptable in adults; dilute for children
Keep an injectable calcium salt (calcium gluconate) immediately available as the antidote
Ensure facilities for assisted ventilation are available during high-dose therapy
moa: Magnesium blocks neuromuscular transmission by decreasing acetylcholine release at the motor end plate and reducing motor end-plate sensitivity; it acts as a physiologic calcium antagonist, depressing the CNS and relaxing smooth and cardiac muscle, which raises the seizure threshold in eclampsia.

relative: Digitalized patients (risk of serious conduction changes)
Concurrent CNS depressants or neuromuscular blockers

preg: Used to prevent and treat eclamptic seizures and as fetal neuroprotection; prolonged use beyond 5-7 days can cause fetal hypocalcemia and skeletal demineralization. Not approved for preterm labor (tocolysis).
lact: Excreted in breast milk in small amounts; considered compatible with breastfeeding.
renal: Reduce dose in renal impairment (e.g., 4 g loading dose then 1 g/hr, max 20 g over 48 h); magnesium is renally excreted and accumulates, raising toxicity risk - monitor serum levels.

major: CNS depressants (opioids, barbiturates, propofol) - potentiated CNS/respiratory depression
Neuromuscular blocking agents - excessive and prolonged neuromuscular blockade
Cardiac glycosides (digoxin) - serious conduction changes/heart block (use with extreme caution)
interactions.diagnostics: Calcium antagonizes magnesium's effects (basis for the calcium antidote); monitor serum magnesium during infusion.

emergency: Loss of patellar reflexes (earliest toxicity sign)

monitoring: Patellar (knee-jerk) reflex must be present before each repeated parenteral dose
Respiratory rate should be at least 16/min before each dose
Urine output at least 100 mL in the 4 hours preceding each dose
Serum magnesium (therapeutic ~2.5-5 mEq/L; reflexes lost ~10 mEq/L; respiratory paralysis hazard)
Continuous fetal heart rate monitoring when used in obstetrics
counsel: This medicine is given by injection or drip in hospital under close monitoring
You may feel warm or flushed during the infusion - this is expected
Tell staff immediately if you feel short of breath, very drowsy, or weak
Monitoring of your reflexes, breathing, and urine is done for your safety
pk: End of IV infusion; ~1 hour after IM
20-25 C; do not use if precipitated or discolored
pearls: Loss of the patellar (knee-jerk) reflex is the earliest clinical sign of toxicity and precedes respiratory depression
IV calcium (calcium gluconate, 10-20 mL of a 10% solution) is the antidote for magnesium toxicity - keep it at the bedside
Magnesium sulphate is superior to phenytoin and diazepam for eclampsia (MAGPIE trial)
Therapeutic serum range for seizure control is roughly 2.5-5 mEq/L (~4.8-8.4 mg/dL)
Reduce the dose and monitor levels closely in renal impairment - the kidney is the sole route of elimination
missed: Administered as a titrated infusion under monitoring - not a self-administered scheduled dose. Hold repeated IM/IV doses if the knee-jerk reflex is absent, respiratory rate is below 16/min, or urine output is inadequate.
overdose: Stop the infusion immediately. Support ventilation. Give IV calcium gluconate (10-20 mL of a 10% solution) as the antidote, repeated as needed. In severe cases or renal failure, magnesium is removed by hemodialysis. Monitor cardiac rhythm, respiration, and serum magnesium.
